fields.h1: Build a Massage Intake Form That Shapes Every Session
fields.hero_description: Tell Emergent what you ask before a session and which answers change it. You get the massage intake form, the rules behind it and a client database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Massage Intake Form Should Handle
fields.features_subheading: Each one answers a question your therapist would otherwise ask with the client already on the table.
fields.feature_1:
Follow-up questions on a tick

Open a follow-up only when a box is ticked. A client who checks recent surgery is asked what was done and when, and one who checks pregnancy is asked how many weeks along.
fields.feature_2:
A body map for focus and no-go areas

Let clients tap the spots to work on and the spots to leave alone, front and back. The marks appear on the therapist's session sheet beside the pressure each client picked.
fields.feature_3:
Answers carried to the next visit

Fill a returning client's form with what they told you last time. They correct the lines that are out of date, and every correction is dated in that client's history.
fields.feature_4:
Holds set by the answers

Hold a booking when an answer needs a conversation first, such as a recent operation. The lead therapist hears about it in Slack or by email before the client arrives.
fields.feature_5:
Consent signed on the last screen

Close the form with your cancellation policy and a consent statement, then collect a typed or drawn signature. The signed copy is saved alongside that visit's answers.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take anywhere

Send the full source of the form and its client database to your GitHub repository. Host it on your own servers, or have a developer wire it into the booking site you use.

fields.usecase_heading: Massage Intake Forms by Practice Type
fields.tab_content_1:
Last visit's answers come back for every regular

Regulars at Stillwater Massage open the intake with last visit's answers already filled in. They confirm what still holds and edit what does not. Leah Moran runs the practice alone, and a new medication or a fresh injury is highlighted at the top of her session sheet before the client walks in.
fields.tab_content_2:
Pregnant guests are booked with prenatal-trained therapists

Juniper Day Spa asks every guest about pregnancy and, on a yes, how many weeks along. A guest at 24 weeks moves from the open Swedish booking to Dana Ellis, who is trained in prenatal massage. The note for Room 3 asks for a side-lying setup with extra pillows.
fields.tab_content_3:
Deep tissue waits for a call after recent knee surgery

Kestrel Sports Massage books deep tissue online, and its intake asks for the date of any surgery in the last 12 weeks. A runner who reports knee surgery 6 weeks ago keeps her slot, but it stays on hold. Owen Tate, the lead therapist, gets a Slack message to call her and confirms the booking after they talk.
fields.tab_content_4:
Each signed form takes the next 15-minute chair slot

On the Globex wellness day, employees scan a QR code at the break room door and answer three screening questions on their phones. Each signed form takes the next open 15-minute slot. Hana Kim works down the list on a tablet, with each person's areas to avoid beside their name.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Massage Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Start from what a therapist needs to know before the session, then decide which answers should change the booking.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Put pressure on the first screen
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about surgery with a date
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Decide who hears about each flag
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down every answer that would change what you do on the table: pressure, areas to avoid, pregnancy, recent surgery and anything the client is allergic to. A question whose answer changes nothing about the session can come off the form.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Place pressure and areas to avoid on the first screen after contact details, because they shape every session. A body map with front and back views is quicker for clients than describing a sore shoulder blade in a text box.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask when an operation happened instead of a yes or no. With a date, the form can tell an operation two years ago from one last month, and only the recent one needs a call before the booking stands.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Name the person who reads each flagged answer: the lead therapist for health questions, the front desk for pregnancy rebookings. Pick Slack or email for each one, and give every flag a fallback for the days that person is off.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your questions and rules into the prompt in plain English. Emergent builds the form, the client database behind it and the alerts. Change a question or a time window later by prompting again, and the live form updates.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Write your cancellation window and late arrival rule in a sentence or two each. Put a consent statement under them and a signature field last. Have a lawyer in your state read any fee you plan to charge before clients sign it.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Send the link with the booking confirmation, then fill it once yourself as a test client who ticks every box. Check that each alert lands. On the day, read the session sheet at the front desk, before the client is in the room.
